[Source 1 — www.kuow.org] (URL: https://www.kuow.org/governing/2026-10-28/kirkland-wants-more-research-before-green-lighting-e-scooters-e-bikes):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Kirkland wants more research before green lighting e-scooters, e-bikes

Cities on Seattle’s Eastside, including Bellevue and Redmond, already allow e-scooters and e-bikes within their city limits, but Kirkland has held out. Now the Kirkland City Council is exploring the possibility, but council members aren’t completely sold on the idea just yet.

Actual Article Body:
A number of cities on Seattle’s Eastside, including Bellevue and Redmond, already allow e-scooters and e-bikes within their city limits, but Kirkland has held out.

Now the Kirkland City Council is exploring the possibility. In August, Lime approached the city about using its bikes and scooters. This month the council decided to study the issue further before taking any action.

Council members agreed it’s not a matter of if Kirkland will allow e-scooters within city limits, but when and how.

“I don’t see it as something that is necessarily a high priority,” Councilmember Jon Pascal said. “We shouldn’t push it off indefinitely given the fact that our surrounding jurisdictions have these micromobility scooters and that they’re already finding their way into our community whether we like them or not.”

According to a staff report, shared electric rides would provide another option for connecting to public transit, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The report also raised concerns about other potential impacts, including clutter, safety, and cost to the city.

One plan under consideration would start a pilot program to explore how shared electric rides might work. The council has opted for additional research to make sure the project complements new rapid bus lines. That would also allow the council to learn from nearby cities. This summer, Bellevue launched an e-scooter and e-bike program through a partnership with Lime.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Flock CEO Wants You To Think Internet Hate For His Company Isn’t Real

‘These people are being paid to say these things’

Actual Article Body:
(Photo by Vincenzo PINTO / AFP) (Photo by VINCENZO PINTO/AFP via Getty Images)

Flock Safety CEO Garrett Langley claimed Sunday, without providing evidence, that online resistance to his company was artificial and created by Russian bots, according to leaked audio obtained by 404 Media.

Langley claimed during the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference in Orlando, Florida, that online protests against Flock were not real and were staged by Russian bots, according to 404 Media. Langley claimed without providing proof that Flock opponents were paid off and that he would prefer never to do an interview with the press again, 404 Media reported.

“These people are being paid to say these things,” Langley said in the leaked audio.

“Online chatter about Flock is down 50% after Ukraine bombed a Russian data center last week […] it’s anonymous bots, and it’s not real,” Langley told the conference, stating his theory that hatred for Flock is astroturfed.

“Whenever this industry finds a highly effective tool, it has to go through this period of intense debate. But then you get on the other side. I think right now we’re not at the bottom, but we’re real, dang-near close to it and about to come back up on the other side,” Langley said.

Flock camera. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Flock Safety is an American company that operates automatic license plate readers (ALPR) and conducts video surveillance. This information can be used to trace people’s whereabouts with precision, raising privacy concerns. Law enforcement can access Flock data without a warrant, according to 404 Media.

There are over 144,000 Flock cameras across the country, according to DeFlock, an open-source project tracking Flock ALPR. (RELATED: Surveillance Patent Shows Flock Spying Way Worse Than Advertised)

Flock Safety did not respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.

Flock protests have occurred across the country as Flock expands its surveillance technology. Barry Harris, a beekeeper from Wilmington, North Carolina, emphasized the bipartisan nature of Flock resistance at an anti-Flock rally in August.

“There’s gays, straights, young, old, liberals, way-left liberals, Genghis Khan conservatives to the right here,” Harris said about the rally’s attendees.

The San Jose Police Department fired an officer who used the Flock network to assist a relative accused of domestic violence in tracking down the alleged victim. A Florida woman was jailed when Flock cameras falsely connected her to a deadly car crash.

“In Milwaukee, prosecutors charged a police officer who allegedly searched his girlfriend’s license plate 124 times and her former boyfriend’s plate 55 times, entering ‘investigation’ as his justification each time,” Republican Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley said in support of Flock regulation.

While Congress hasn’t proposed any bills to outright ban Flock cameras, several bills would restrict the use of Flock surveillance data. Independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders proposed a bill to restrict federal funding for Flock, and Hawley introduced a bill to prevent the sharing of Flock data with non-governmental third parties.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Trump administration wants to remove regulations on a super planet-heating gas

The Trump administration wants to undo a Biden-era rule that would reduce methane emissions from the oil and gas industry.

Actual Article Body:
By

Julia Simon

,

Kirk Siegler

Flares burn off methane and other hydrocarbons at an oil and gas facility in Lenorah, Texas, Oct. 15, 2021.
                
                    
                    David Goldman/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

The Trump administration is proposing to dramatically scale back a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut methane emissions from the oil and gas industry at drilling sites nationwide.

Methane is a major contributor to climate change and is estimated to be 80 times more planet-warming than carbon dioxide in a twenty-year time frame. In 2023, the Biden administration finalized rules that were meant to rein in methane emissions from the oil and gas sector.

President Trump made the announcement while campaigning in Lubbock, Texas, Tuesday, saying his administration's revision, under the Clean Air Act, would save the industry billions in production costs and spur more domestic drilling. The proposal comes as Republicans face a backlash from voters over high gas prices heading into the midterms.

"Behind every barrel of oil and every cubic foot of natural gas produced in the U.S. are millions of workers, businesses, and the heartbeat of this nation's economy. The Biden EPA destructively targeted all this," EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a press release.

The oil and gas industry, which vigorously opposed the 2023 rules, said EPA's proposed rollback will address some of the challenges companies have faced in trying to comply with the regulations.

"We look forward to working with the Trump administration on a more workable approach that supports American energy production, provides greater regulatory certainty and advances continued emissions reductions," Dustin Meyer, vice president at the American Petroleum Institute, a trade organization for the U.S. oil and gas industry, said in a statement.

But environmentalists say this may end up actually costing the industry more.

"Methane is natural gas, or natural gas is methane," says Jon Goldstein, associate vice president at the Environmental Defense Fund. "And so if you're capturing more natural gas, you're not allowing it to leak out, you're not allowing it to be flared, you have more product that you can sell. And so that offsets a lot of the costs."

"That is harmful to our energy security, and it's harmful to taxpayers that ought to be seeing royalty and tax revenue collected off of this gas that's going to waste," Goldstein adds.

One of the regulations the EPA wants to cut is the "Methane Super Emitter Program." Across the U.S., oil and gas pipelines, refineries, and other energy facilities sometimes have huge leaks of methane. But methane is invisible and difficult, not to mention expensive, to detect. The super emitter program is supposed to take effect in January 2027. It would allow the government to delegate monitoring for big methane leaks to certified third parties, including private and nonprofit methane satellite programs.

"The easiest way to think about it is that if the government is alerted to a big leak, then if it's reported by certified third parties, then they could use that information," says Paasha Mahdavi, a political science professor at UC Santa Barbara who studies the oil industry.

"[The government] needs help from other people to say, 'Hey! You're breaking the law!' so they're able to prosecute," Mahdavi adds.

If that program goes away, Mahdavi says it will be harder for the government to spot large leaks of the planet-heating gas from oil and gas facilities. "And we need that because it's really hard to see this stuff," he says.

The EPA's announcement would also loosen regulations on methane leaks coming from low-volume "marginal" oil wells that are considered "marginally economic," meaning they don't make much money.

"People assume marginal well must equal small emissions," Goldstein says. But he says satellites and new technology find that's not true. "These old sort of end-of-life wells nearing the end of their production life are actually responsible for the lion's share of methane pollution from the [oil and gas] production sector," Goldstein says.

The EPA plans to hold at least a 45-day public comment period, including a public hearing, once the proposed rule changes are published in the Federal Register.
